A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the gut microbial flora of resistant mice is able to maintain its balance with S. enterica during a latent carrier state, and that this balance may be due in part to the production of interferon gamma.

the microbiota of the ileocecum of resistant mice is not affected by S. enterica infection, as the microbiota of infected animals is very similar to the microbiota of control animals, and the microbiota of all the animals is very stable over time.

we have shown that S. enteritidis is capable of colonizing the gut in a resistant mouse model, and we have demonstrated that the microbial community is altered in the first 3 days post-inoculated, but that it is restored to a normal state after 28 days.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the gut microbiota is not a static entity, and it is not possible to predict the composition of the microbiota of a given host based on the composition of the host’s gut microbiota at a given point in time.
the gut microbiota of the mouse can tolerate a S. Enteritidis colonization for at least 28 days.
the microbiota of mice infected with Salmonella enterica is not completely disrupted by the infection.
